item.title: How lab-grown diamonds have changed the game
item.description: The saying goes that ‘diamonds are forever’. But what if the market for them isn’t?
item.content:encoded:
You’ve probably heard the saying “a diamond is forever”. What if the market for them – with its hefty price tags – isn’t?

Back in March, Rio Tinto ended production at its Diavik diamond mine in Canada after 23 years. Earlier this month, diamond mining company De Beers announced a two-year production pause at the company’s flagship Venetia mine in South Africa.

De Beers is majority-owned by global mining giant Anglo American. According to a Bloomberg report this week, Anglo is now in talks to sell its 85% stake for about US$1 billion – a tiny fraction of the US$18 billion it was valued at when taken private in 2001.

So, what’s going on? The industry certainly hasn’t run out of diamonds to mine. But current prices and costs have made continued production of natural diamonds harder to justify.

Over the past couple of decades, lab-grown diamonds have changed the game. Consumers are also reconsidering what makes a diamond valuable – and what responsible consumption means.

A lesson from aluminium

In the mid-nineteenth century, aluminium was treated as a luxury material and its value exceeded that of gold. While it was abundant in the Earth’s crust, it was difficult and expensive to isolate and refine.

item.title: Who was Homer, author of the ‘Odyssey’?
item.description: When the ‘Odyssey’ first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.
item.content:encoded:
Who wrote the Odyssey?

Homer, obviously: that is what we’ve been told since the late 6th century BCE, when ancient Greeks started crediting the Odyssey to a blind bard from the rocky isle of Chios.

But this “Homer” appeared at least a century later than the poem itself. When the Odyssey first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.

How can you have a poem without a poet? Two American researchers, Milman Parry and Albert Lord, came across a possible answer.

In the 1930s, Parry and Lord travelled to the Balkans to study still-living traditions of epic poetry. In Yugoslavia and Albania, they found bards who sang of heroes from long ago. These singers did not recite from a book. Most of them couldn’t read or write at all. Instead, they improvised their epics as they sang. They knew the story by heart, but told it in different words with each performance.

Balkan bards achieved this by relying on a stock of formulaic scenes, lines and phrases, which they combined on the spot. The formulae were passed down from teacher to student, so that all singers tended to sound alike.

This telltale style is just what we find in Homeric poetry....

item.title: Can fuel-reliant South Asia survive the next global conflict?
item.description: The oil-importing countries of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka must invest in building energy security.
item.content:encoded:
Amid signs that the US and Iran have paused their latest round of hostilities, it is time to examine the economies that the conflict effectively brought to a standstill this year.

In March 2026, when the exchange of threats and missiles choked the Strait of Hormuz, the bill landed on the doors of Dhaka, Islamabad and Colombo long before it reached Washington or Brussels.

The moment revealed itself less as a geopolitical crisis and more as unending queues for fuel in South Asia, with restaurants shuttered and households plunged into darkness by relentless load shedding.

Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka – three countries with virtually no domestic oil reserves and no meaningful influence over global commodity prices – absorbed energy shocks for a war they did not cause. That is the nature of fossil-fuel dependence in South Asia, and it is not new. The 2008 oil price bubble and subsequent spike. The 2022 Russia‑Ukraine war in which Russia limited supplies and caused gas price shocks. These are other chapters in the same structural story.

What makes 2026 different is that alternatives now exist, they are affordable, and some of these countries have already begun deploying them. The question is whether they build on that foundation proactively before the next disruption, or patch the damage reactively...

item.title: Rahul Gandhi, 2 MPs booked for ‘insulting Sanatan Dharma’ during Ram temple donation theft protest
item.description: An FIR was filed in Varanasi after Opposition leaders enacted a skit outside Parliament depicting the alleged embezzlement of donations made to the Ram temple.

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and two other Opposition MPs have been booked in Uttar Pradesh’s Varanasi for allegedly insulting Sanatan Dharma during a protest outside Parliament, The Hindu reported.

Sanatana Dharma is a term some people use as a synonym for Hinduism.

On Friday, INDIA bloc MPs, including Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Gandhi, staged a protest over the alleged embezzlement of donations made to the Ram temple in Ayodhya.

During the protest, the MPs enacted a skit. They dropped money into a donation box, while Independent MP Pappu Yadav, dressed in saffron robes, pretended to take the money out and put it into his pockets.

On Saturday, a first information report was registered at Kotwali police station against Gandhi, the leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Yadav and Samajwadi Party MP Awadhesh Prasad.

They have been charged under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita pertaining to deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings and uttering words with the deliberate intent to wound the religious feelings of any person, the newspaper reported.

item.title: Anti-paper leak amendments become law after president’s assent
item.description: The legislation was introduced in Parliament on Monday following nationwide youth protests about alleged irregularities in competitive examinations.
item.content:encoded:
President Droupadi Murmu on Friday gave her assent to the 2026 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Act, a day after Parliament passed the legislation.

The amendments were introduced on Monday following nationwide youth protests over alleged irregularities in competitive examinations.

The Act raises the punishment for using unfair means in public examinations from the current three to five years’ imprisonment to five to 10 years. It also increases the maximum fine from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.

One of the key provisions of the Act empowers the Union government to set up a Special Task Force to investigate paper leak offences. The probe by police, central investigating agencies or the task force would have to be completed within two months, it says.

The Act also requires state governments and Union Territory administrations to set up special fast track courts. Pending cases under the Act would also be transferred to these fast track courts and disposed of within three months of transfer.

If instances of paper leaks or other offences listed under the Act are found to be organised, the legislation proposes a minimum sentence of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.

item.title: ‘The Business of Business Is Not Just Business’: A changing view of Indian corporate responsibility
item.description: The anthology brings together a diverse and accomplished set of minds to study how business can shape culture.
item.content:encoded:
The title of Sutapa Banerjee’s edited volume, The Business of Business Is (Not) Just Business, underlines something that few would argue against. The era when businesses could legitimately argue that the only responsibility they have is to their shareholders is behind us. The role of business is widely acknowledged to encompass a much larger range of stakeholders. Businesses are not exempt from society; they play an active role in shaping it not just in economic terms but also culturally. Employment, migration, gender, environment, aspirations, access to opportunity, public discourse and the very idea of progress are all shaped in some way or the other by business.

And the book’s declared intention is to examine this from the lens of behaviour on the ground. What actually shapes behaviour, what exactly is meant by change, what mechanisms help produce this change at ground level?

Building businesses

It brings together a diverse and accomplished set of minds to study these questions. The contributors include business leaders, investors, policymakers and domain specialists across questions of sustainability, inclusion, employment, gender, technology and corporate governance. Its range is considerable. item.title: Commentator Tehseen Poonawalla claims he is under house arrest ahead of protest against E20 fuel
item.description: He had been scheduled to begin a hunger strike in Delhi at 10 am.
item.content:encoded:
Political commentator Tehseen Poonawalla on Saturday alleged that police had put him under house arrest at his home in Delhi ahead of his planned protest against petrol being blended with 20% ethanol.

Poonawalla was scheduled to begin a hunger strike at the Gandhi Smriti in the national capital at 10 am, to protest against the government’s Ethanol Blended Petrol programme.

The Union government has mandated that all petrol sold in the country be blended with 20% ethanol – a substance produced from sugarcane and food grain. The policy is aimed at reducing India’s dependency on fossil fuels, cutting greenhouse gas emissions and boosting income for sugarcane farmers.

However, consumers have complained that the new fuel mix damages engines and reduces their mileage.

Speaking with reporters on Saturday, Poonawalla claimed that the police informed him that he had been put under house arrest because “thousands of protesters” were expected to participate in the protest.

The police did not give him any documents explaining the action, Poonawalla alleged.

“An entire battalion of Delhi Police cops including women officers have put me under house arrest!” Poonawalla alleged on social media, adding that Nitin Gadkari, the Union transport minister “is scared” of the protest against the ethanol policy.

item.title: August Indian nonfiction: Six new titles that take a closer look at 79 years of independence
item.description: A journalist’s report from India’s Maoist hotbed, a genius mathematician’s biography, an examination of India’s social policy, and more.
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

DD Kosambi: One Life Many Worlds, Ram Ramaswamy

Historian. Mathematician. Marxist. Polymath. DD Kosambi defied labels. The range and intellectual heft of his scholarship was truly astounding, with fundamental contributions in differential geometry and analyses in mathematics, the Kosambi distance in genetics, a statistical analysis of ancient coin hoards, a radical reinterpretation of Indian history and stellar compilations of the poetry of Vidyakara and Bhartrhari-all this in addition to a firm commitment to world peace and environmental activism.

Yet, for a man who contributed so much to the Indian intellectual tradition, he remains largely unknown. Sixty years after his passing, there is scant recognition of his talents-he is quoted more often than he is read and praised more often than he is analysed.

Ram Ramaswamy’s biography of Kosambi seeks to correct this lapse. Set against the backdrop of fascinating social, political, scientific and historiographical transformation in the subcontinent, and drawing from letters, journal entries, family accounts and unprecedented archival material, DD Kosambi: One Life, Many Worlds reveals a rare incandescent genius and a fearless independent spirit with boundless curiosity-whose relevance in the fields of pedagogy, research and invention can be seen even today.

Data shared by the Election Commission showed that only 77% of the enumeration forms had been digitised in the state as of Friday. The digitisation rate was 56.3% in Hyderabad.

Yadadri Bhongiri district had recorded the highest form digitisation rate of 94.2%, followed by Jangaon at 91.4%.

item.title: The story of Kerala’s first female writer-composer who transcended her time
item.description: Kuttykunju Thangkachi broke new ground in music, theatre and literature at a time when women’s creativity was expected to remain private.
item.content:encoded:
A gaunt elderly woman, her face sombre and framed by wispy grey hair left loose over her shoulders, gazes out in the side-profile. She wears the unmistakable symbols of an upper caste elite woman from 19th-century Kerala: the mundu mulakacha wrap tied across her chest, layers of gold around her neck, and a yawning ear piercing that signals a lifetime of wearing heavy gold earrings. Yet to dismiss Kuttykunju Thangkachi as merely a privileged noblewoman would be a profound mistake.

The tumultuous 84 years of her life, which ended in 1904, were packed with triumphs virtually unheard of for women of her era. She was the earliest female dramatist in Malayalam with her play Ajnatavasam, the first woman to write attakathas, or librettos, for Kathakali, and a prolific creator across Kerala’s indigenous musical forms, including kummi, thiruvathira pattu, kurathipattu and thullal. Crucially, she was the first female Carnatic composer from Kerala at a time when only men were accorded the elevated title of vaggeyakara (writer-composer).

item.title: J&K: Second migrant worker succumbs to injuries sustained in Kulgam militant attack
item.description: Another labourer had died in the attack on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
A migrant worker succumbed to his injuries sustained during a suspected militant attack in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district on Friday.

The labourer had been taken to a hospital in Srinagar.

Another migrant worker had died in the attack on Friday. Both were from Chhattisgarh.

The suspected militants had opened fire at them in the Kellam area of Kulgam. Following the attack, the security forces cordoned off the area and began a search operation to track down the assailants.

Following the attack, Jammu and Kashmir Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha condemned the attack, and said that he had spoken to Director General of Police Nalin Prabhat and other security officers.

The lieutenant governor said that he had directed the security forces “to step up their operations and eliminate the terrorists”.

On Saturday, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah announced an ex-gratia payment of Rs 10 lakh each to families of the two workers. Additionally, the district administration will provide immediate assistance of Rs 6 lakh each, the chief minister’s office said

The attack came a week after a policeman was killed when militants opened fire on security personnel in Jammu and Kashmir’s Anantnag district on July 22. The policeman was identified as Head Constable Ashiq Hussain Qureshi.

The external affairs minister also said that he was apprised of Tehran’s “perspective of the current developments and discussions underway” and that New Delhi supports dialogue and diplomacy to ensure peace in West Asia.

item.title: ‘We will kill, rape you’: Online mobs are targeting women protesters for ‘abusing’ Modi
item.description: BJP supporters are doxing protestors from Jantar Mantar even as FIRs are filed against them. But Modi has said they need to be shown the ‘right way’.
item.content:encoded:
When Shradha Singh created an Instagram reel alongside two Rapid Action Force personnel in Connaught Place, she had no idea the seven-second clip would be weaponised against her.

The 23-year-old content creator and yoga instructor from Madhya Pradesh was part of the growing crowd of young people who converged on New Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in the third week of July to express anger against question paper leaks. Like many others, Singh had seen the Indian public examinations system up close and had grown disillusioned with it. This prompted her to turn up to support the protesting students.

Today, she cannot step outside her home.

Her ordeal is part of a chilling new reality unfolding for young protesters in the capital. Their open – and sometimes abusive – challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Bharatiya Janata Party has made them the targets of relentless harassment from both online mobs as well as the police.

item.title: Avni Doshi’s ‘The First House’: When the forced end of a marriage horrifyingly annihilates the self
item.description: Doshi’s new novel banishes once and for all any assumptions that a ‘good’ woman is promised happiness.
item.content:encoded:
Booker Prize-shortlisted author Avni Doshi’s new novel, The First House, is here. And it is magnificent. A terrifying story of heartbreak, humiliation, and total annihilation of the self, the novel burns through the skin, scorching the very heart.

The novel starts with the narrator’s husband asking for a divorce. She had believed them to be reasonably happy, but after two daughters, the husband would beg to differ. The reasons are the usual – he feels trapped, he’s bored, the wife is too much. She proceeds to remind him of his responsibilities, especially towards his children. It’s a deadlock. The marriage is over.

It happens at a time of cicadas bursting out of their cocoons and the couple’s planets behaving erratically. The end of the marriage, in these circumstances, is presented almost like a natural occurrence.

Bye bye, baby

The immediate aftermath comprises dealing with the children, the possibility of the husband’s having an affair, the narrator’s work-in-progress novel facing yet another setback, and, worst of all, money troubles. Panic shot through me each time the narrator’s credit card was declined (it is managed by her husband) and she dug around for cash. item.title: ‘The Good Reporter’: The women journalists of Khabar Lahariya tell their stories on their own terms
item.description: The ‘journalism memoir’ is written by ten women from the Khabar Lahariya collective, alongside journalist and co-founder Disha Mullick.
item.content:encoded:
At some point in the early years of Khabar Lahariya, a story about a stolen buffalo calf made the front page. The women who put it there understood that the theft of a calf in rural UP was not a minor story dressed up as news. It was a story about inter-caste harassment, about whose losses count and who gets to decide what the public needs to investigate. The Good Reporter: A Memoir of Journalism in the 21st Century is a memoir about journalism built on that understanding.

The book opens with a warning. “This is a somewhat elliptical, unreliable autobiography of ten very different women,” it says before you have properly settled in. The story of what this collective has done over two decades of rural journalism in UP “has always been a better story to tell than how we have done it and keep doing it.” That distinction between the what versus the how is what the entire book turns on. If you came for the rousing version, the collective has already clocked you.

Amid police cases against youth protesters for social media posts making purportedly objectionable remarks about him, PM Narendra Modi on Friday said that he wants to forgive the students.

“The country and the world witnessed what happened at Jantar Mantar,” he said in a video posted on social media. “Some mischievous children used abusive language that doesn’t dignify any civilised society. They not only abused me but even my late mother.”

Modi said that a person can make an error of judgement when they are young, but such mistakes can be corrected.

“I understand the anger in our society,” Modi said. “There is a cultural shock about our daughters using such language. This is the time to show them the right path. They are misguided.”

The prime minister appealed for restraint from the public, saying that making the student protesters run around courts will not provide solutions to problems.

“I want to forgive them,” Modi said. “The children are ours and we have to show them the right path even if it is difficult to do to people who have been misled,” he added.

item.title: Saffron shadows: Hockey India should have adopted the three-colour football kit of 1984
item.description: Dressing the national team in the signature colour of the BJP-RSS cloaks the squads in a shade freighted with politics and sectarianism.
item.content:encoded:
January 13,1984: I was 16, and it was the first football match I had watched with my own eyes rather than through the grain of a Doordarshan transmission. My father and I were among the 80,000 football fans crowded into Eden Gardens, for a Nehru Cup encounter between an unfancied India and mighty Argentina.

A video clip of that game resurfaced on YouTube a couple of weeks ago and refreshed three of my lasting memories of the game. The first is of disappointment: Diego Maradona, already reckoned to be the best player of his generation, had stayed home. But the Argentines were not lacking in quality. Carlos Bilardo was in the dugout, and his team that evening included Nery Pumpido, Oscar Garré, Ricardo Giusti and Jorge Burruchaga, all of whom would be World Cup winners in Mexico two years later.

The Indian team may have lacked players of that class, but it had a coach of genuine international pedigree: Milovan Ćirić of Yugoslavia (as it was then) who had managed Lazio and Valencia.

item.title: In Nicaragua, President Ortega bans elections – a new page in the authoritarian playbook
item.description: This shows a growing brazenness among autocratic regimes and a declining concern for international legitimacy.
item.content:encoded:
Since being elected for a second term as Nicaraguan president in 2006, Daniel Ortega – the former Sandinista freedom fighter-turned-authoritarian leader – has extended his term of office several times. But last week he announced a new strategy for holding on to power.

He declared that there will no longer be elections in the Central American country. Making a speech to commemorate the anniversary of the 1979 revolution that toppled the Somoza dictatorship which had ruled Nicaragua since 1937, he said: “The days when parties backed by the Yankees and the Somocistas would return to power are over – never again.” The legal changes are already moving through the country’s legislature.

Nicaragua’s elections have long been rigged and repressive. But this marks a new scale of authoritarian rule. The elimination of elections is a rare and extreme case, even in today’s landscape of authoritarian regimes. So this reflects a worrying trend of brazenness on the part of Nicaragua’s president.

Spin dictators

Most modern autocrats are what researchers call “spin dictators”. They invest in a democratic disguise and the careful curation of a public image fostered by propaganda and misinformation. Elections play a central role in this playbook.

item.title: Deluge with monsoon deficit is India’s new climate normal
item.description: Climate change is no longer about more or less rainfall but is redistributing water in increasingly unpredictable ways.
item.content:encoded:
In the first week of July, in Mumbai’s Mankhurd, torrential monsoon rains triggered a building collapse that buried five children beneath the debris, transforming one of the city’s wettest July days in half a century into a humanitarian tragedy. Streets disappeared beneath floodwaters, transport networks ground to a halt, and emergency services struggled to reach stranded residents.

Thousands of kilometres away, London faced an entirely different manifestation of the same crisis. During the June 2026 heatwave, temperatures exceeded 36 degrees celsius, commuters fainted inside sweltering Underground trains, and climate activists covered Tube stations with stickers reading, “Heatwave, sponsored by Shell”, highlighting the perceived role of fossil fuels in intensifying global warming.

These events unfolded in vastly different economic and geographic settings. Yet they reflected a common reality: climate change no longer distinguishes between developed and developing nations. Whether through floods, heatwaves, landslides or dust storms, extreme weather is increasingly becoming the defining challenge of the twenty-first century.

The scientific evidence underpinning this reality has become overwhelming. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) reported in 2023 that the global mean near-surface temperature in 2023 was 1.45 ± 0.12 degrees celsius above the pre-industrial average, bringing the world dangerously close to the 1.5 degrees celsius threshold established under the Paris Agreement.

item.title: Three reasons why India’s household savings are falling despite a huge working-age population
item.description: Families are borrowing money for consumption, a sign of poor-quality, low-paying jobs while instruments to create savings are inadequate.
item.content:encoded:
India’s demographic dividend of a large, youthful workforce is being unsettled by a troubled trend: even as the share of working-age Indians climbs to record highs, household savings have fallen to their lowest level in nearly two decades.

This puzzle strikes at the heart of an influential economic theory.

In 1985, Franco Modigliani won the Nobel Prize for his life-cycle hypothesis of household savings. People spread out their consumption across a lifetime: borrowing when young, saving hard through their prime working years and drawing down those savings in retirement.

On a population scale, Modigliani’s theory implies that a country’s saving rate depends less on its wealth and more on how its people are distributed across the life cycle.

A nation with a bulge of prime-age workers should save a lot. Economists Ronald Lee and Andrew Mason later sharpened this insight into what they called the “second demographic dividend”.

The first dividend – the one India routinely celebrates – is the mechanical boost to output per person that comes from a rising share of working-age people. The second is subtler and, crucially, not guaranteed. It materialises only where pensions, formal financial systems and functioning labour markets allow the instinct to save for later life to translate into real, investable wealth.

item.description: Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest number of deaths at 10.
item.content:encoded:
Forty-seven sanitation workers died while cleaning sewers and septic tanks across India in 2025, the Union government said on Wednesday.

Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest number of deaths at 10, followed by Haryana with seven and Tamil Nadu with six, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment said in response to an MP’s question.

Manual scavenging – the practice of removing human excreta by hand from sewer lines or septic tanks – is banned under the 2013 Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act. However, the practice remains prevalent in several parts of the country.

Responding to a question on the effectiveness of existing laws, Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Ramdas Athawale said that the scheme was evaluated in 2025. He added that it provides sanitation workers with safety equipment, occupational training, health insurance and financial support to promote mechanisation of the process.

The government said that states and Union Territories have been asked to ensure that the 2013 law is implemented.. It also noted that the Union housing and urban affairs ministry had issued standard operating procedures for cleaning sewers and septic tanks.

The decision of the Indian hockey federation to change the colour of the team’s jersey to saffron from blue has drawn criticism, with former captain Viren Rasquinha describing the change as embarrassing.

“The legacy and identity of the Indian team has always been blue,” he said on social media on Wednesday. “I wore the blue jersey with pride for many years. Fans want to see our Indian team in blue. What is the logic of orange?”

The hockey federation launched the new jersey on Monday. In a social media video, the federation said that the saffron colour “symbolises courage, sacrifice and victory”.

The new colours scheme has been inspired by the national flag and the rising sun, it said, adding that the new jersey “reflects new beginnings”.

Several social media users criticised the colour blue being replaced with saffron, saying that the change hurts the team’s legacy and identity.

India has traditionally had blue as the colour of the primary jersey. The country’s sports teams are often called by fans as the “men in blue” or “women in blue”.

Following the backlash, Hockey India said on Thursday that the change had been made following consultations with players and the staff because of technical requirements.

The farmers were demanding 100% procurement of moong at the minimum support price.

Farmer organisations have said that while the Union government has announced full procurement of tur, urad and masur, moong continues to be procured under the price support scheme, in which purchases are capped at 25% of a state’s estimated production, The Indian Express reported.

They argued that the ceiling forces farmers to sell much of their harvest in the open market at prices below the minimum support price.

The agitation began on Monday, when farmers from 19 organisations under the banner of the Samyukta Kisan Morcha began a march towards Bhopal from Sethani Ghat in Narmadapuram 75 km away.

item.title: Why an Aadhaar fix for India’s education crisis won’t work
item.description: Technocratic solutions conflate logistical efficiency with social equity and cannot substitute for democratic reforms.
item.content:encoded:
The government’s recurring policy response is to deal with institutional failures as software problems. The assumption is that securing the platform, digitising the database and centralising management under technocrats will solve social problems. Therefore, let us bring in the master engineer to re-code the system.

Similarly, the government has now constituted a “high-powered task force” headed by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani to recommend examination reforms. It follows nearly two months of protests by students and youngsters against the leak of the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for admission to undergraduate medical courses.

This approach conflates logistical efficiency with social equity.

It is a manifestation of a deep, chronic flaw in the ruling establishment’s imagination that socio-political crises can be engineered away through top-down, technocratic management.

Lessons from Aadhaar

India’s Aadhaar experiment supplies ample empirical evidence of why a purely technocratic approach to education and examinations is dangerous. In 2009, when Nilekani was brought in to build Aadhaar, the promise was similar: a frictionless, fraud-proof, digital architecture that would eliminate corruption and streamline the welfare state.

Instead, it was a classic case of technocratic hubris. Aadhaar’s real-world implementation subordinated human rights to digital server uptime while storing vast amounts of personal data in leaky systems.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday quashed a 2021 office memorandum that created a mechanism for the Union government to grant environmental clearances to projects that had commenced operations without obtaining an approval, Live Law reported.

The court held that the government cannot introduce such a scheme through an administrative order.

It also noted that the government has the power to provide for retrospective environmental clearances through a statutory notification issued under the 1986 Environment Protection Act.

A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, in a unanimous verdict, held that the judgement would apply prospectively, meaning that the projects that had been given post-facto environmental clearances will not be affected.

The bench also said that the Union government has power under the Environment Protection Act to issue notifications that would allow certain categories of projects that began without getting an environmental clearance to obtain a retrospective approval in the larger public interest, PTI reported.

The projects include the AIIMS Medical College and Hospital building in Odisha, the Centre of Excellence for Cancer Diseases in Tamil Nadu, the Vijayapura airport in Karnataka, slum rehabilitation projects and irrigation projects intended for drought-prone areas.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has held public office for nearly a quarter of a century, has been humbled by a band of protesters, most of whom have not even spent that much time on the planet yet. For the first time in almost eight years, public pressure has forced a powerful minister in his cabinet to step down.

The development assumes greater significance because the social group that managed to pull this off has never possessed bargaining power of this sort in Indian history. A ragtag coalition of young Indians – under the banner of the “Cockroach Janta Party” – that somehow stuck together and stayed on the streets of Delhi for five weeks through the scorching summer heat to demand accountability for corruption in India’s public examination system has made Modi blink.

item.title: How Latin America’s rightwing politicians use humour to normalise their extremist ideologies
item.description: Their jokes undermine public trust in institutions, encourage reactionary movements and weaken social cohesion by fostering division.
item.content:encoded:
Humour plays a key role in the political communication of rightwing populist leaders in Latin America. Politicians including Javier Milei in Argentina, Nayib Bukele in El Salvador and Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil have all used humour to engage with and solidify their support base, normalise extreme ideologies and deflect criticism.

Humour also circulates constantly among their followers. In October 2022, a few months before Brazilians went to the polls in their last general election, I carried out fieldwork at a Bolsonaro rally in the Brazilian city of Rio de Janeiro with a group of colleagues.

We overheard a Bolsonaro supporter joking about a stray dog. “Watch out for that dog!” he shouted. “If Lula wins, we’ll have to call him picanha [a type of beef].”

The crowd laughed, with another supporter adding: “If Lula wins, he’ll be the first to eat it.” Lula went on to be elected as Brazil’s president by a razor-thin margin.

Argentina held elections the following year to appoint successors to President Alberto Fernández and his vice-president, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner – who had dominated Argentinian politics for two decades alongside her husband, Néstor Kirchner. Together, they had forged Kirchnerism, the country’s main leftwing populist movement.

Narayanan R stood on the muddy bund of the Great Salt Lake, watching a group of flamingoes pick their way across the shallows. He remembered standing in the same spot as a 10-year-old, knee-deep in water – the day his father showed him how to fish. “The flamingoes may not come next season,” he said. “These pools will dry soon.

A few hundred metres away, Gowriamma waded through the shallow waters of the lake, her fingers sifting through the mud for shrimp. “Everything depends on these small pools. We know this water through the mud and the thorns.”

Located between Nemmeli and Kovalam in Chennai, the Great Salt Lake also known as Kovalam-Nemmeli backwaters, is a coastal wetland that spans 5,000 acres. The Tamil Nadu government plans to convert this coastal wetland into Chennai’s sixth drinking water reservoir: the Mamallan reservoir.

Chennai currently supplies between 700 and 800 million litres per day of water. The Booker Prize announced its 2025 longlist of thirteen titles on Tuesday. The longlisted authors represent seven countries and three continents. Past winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart and previously shortlisted author Elizabeth Strout are on this year’s longlist, alongside ten authors who are longlisted for the first time – including three debut novelists.

Should either James or Stuart win this year, they’ll join an elite list of four authors who have won the Booker Prize twice: JM Coetzee (1983 and 1999), Peter Carey (1988 and 2001), Hilary Mantel (2009 and 2012) and Margaret Atwood (2000 and 2019).

The shortlist will be announced on September 22, and the winner, on November 9. The winner will receive £50,000, while the shortlisted authors will each receive £2,500.

This year’s jury is chaired by writer Mary Beard, and she’s joined by writer and educator Raymond Antrobus; musician, writer and broadcaster Jarvis Cocker; journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu; and Booker Prize-shortlisted novelist Patricia Lockwood.

Announcing the longlist, Beard said, “Great books have never been written to a single formula. We are confident that our longlist of books has something for everyone. There’s the funny and the unsettling (and in some cases the funny and unsettling); there’s dystopian fantasy and domestic drama;...

item.title: Bill to amend anti-paper leak law passed in Lok Sabha after nationwide protests
item.description: The legislation was passed amid slogans by the Opposition MPs, demanding ‘justice’ for the students who took part in the march to Parliament on July 20.
item.content:encoded:
The Lok Sabha on Wednesday passed a bill to amend the anti-paper leak law through a voice vote.

The bill will now be moved to the Rajya Sabha. If cleared by the Upper House of Parliament, it will be sent for presidential assent.

The 2026 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Bill was introduced by Union minister Jitendra Singh on Monday, days after nationwide protests against alleged irregularities in the conduct of competitive examinations.

The legislation proposes imprisonment of five to ten years for individuals found using unfair means in public examinations. The maximum fine for such persons would increase from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.

Speaking in the Lok Sabha, Singh said that the government took swift action in the 2026 National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test paper leak case. He added that 52 first information reports had been lodged since the 2024 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Act came into force.

The bill was passed amid slogans by the Opposition MPs, demanding “justice” for the students who took part in the march to Parliament on July 20. Dozens were injured as the police used lathis, fired tear gas shells and pellet guns against the demonstrators.

The House was adjourned for the day following the passage of the bill.

item.title: Fiction: Demon queen Ayasi’s wrath will consume the mountain kingdom struggling to appease her
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Ayasi: The Wandering Death’, by Tanvi Singh.
item.content:encoded:
Chief Monk Lobsang leaves the Sarnai Monastery at twilight sans parting ceremony or retinue. It isn’t a joyous occasion to require as much. Climbing down the ancient, worn-out ladder that connected the Sarnai Monastery to Mang Yul strains his old bones, but he carries on.

He chooses to not traverse through the deadwood of the Baika Forest, but rather skirt around it, evading the shrine of the tutelary deities of the forest – 30 smooth stones smeared with red ochre and cordoned off with ropes – heading for the small pastoral village of Bayarma, south of the capital. The new capital, Lobsang corrects himself.

item.title: SC accepts CBI’s decision to clear ex-PM Manmohan Singh in alleged coal scam case
item.description: A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant allowed Singh’s appeal challenging the summons issued to him by a trial court in 2015.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday accepted the Central Bureau of Investigation’s decision to close the case against former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh in an alleged coal allocation scam, Bar and Bench reported.

A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant allowed Singh’s appeal challenging the summons issued to him by a trial court in 2015.

The order came a year-and-a-half after the former prime minister died in December 2024.

On Wednesday, advocate Kapil Sibal told the court that while Singh’s appeal may have technically become infructuous, or no longer relevant, after his death, the trial court’s adverse observations against the former prime minister required judicial interference, Live Law reported. Sibal urged the court to expunge those observations.

The Supreme Court remarked that although Singh’s death meant that the appeal could be disposed of as infructuous, it was important to look into whether the trial court’s decision to summon him was legally valid.

The bench noted that the special judge had rejected the CBI’s closure report on Singh, and taken cognisance of the case under the Prevention of Corruption Act, Live Law reported. The court said that the special judge had failed to apply settled principles about the acceptance of closure reports.

item.title: Slow trial violates right to liberty: SC grants bail to two UAPA suspects after 12 years in custody
item.description: Mohammed Saquib Ansari and Waqar Azhar were arrested by the Delhi Police Special Cell in 2014 over alleged links to an Indian Mujahideen module.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday granted bail to two men who had been in jail for 12 years under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, observing that there was no immediate prospect of the trial concluding, Live Law reported.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta held that the continued incarceration of the suspects amounted to a violation of their fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

The court has directed the release on bail of Mohammed Saquib Ansari and Waqar Azhar, subject to conditions imposed by the trial court and provided they were not required in any other case, the legal news outlet reported.

The case stems from the arrest of a suspected Indian Mujahideen member in November 2011, who allegedly disclosed the existence of a Rajasthan module of the banned outfit during interrogation.

Justice Madhav Jamdar added that citizens are entitled to hold different opinions and quashed externment orders banning two members of the Social Democratic Party of India from entering Mumbai for a period of one year.

The Babri Masjid was demolished on December 6, 1992, by Hindu extremists because they believed that it stood on the spot on which the deity Ram had been born. They may face emotional neglect, physical abuse andlong-lasting struggles with trust, self-esteem and mental health.


Pallavi, 24, came to us with severe depression, an eating disorder and intense anger. In rage, she would bang her head or hit herself.

“There is nobody for me in this world,” she said quietly.

She also struggled with compulsive needs around bathrooms and cleanliness, something she felt too ashamed to tell anyone. Even though she was an only child, she felt emotionally distant, almost disconnected, from both parents.

item.title: Assam flood toll rises to 75
item.description: Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma increased the ex gratia payment for the families of those killed in the floods to Rs 9 lakh from Rs 4 lakh.
item.content:encoded:
The toll in flood-related incidents in Assam rose to 75 on Tuesday after seven more deaths were reported in Sivasagar district, the state disaster management authority said.

Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Tuesday announced that the ex gratia payment for the families of those killed in the floods had been increased to Rs 9 lakh from Rs 4 lakh. An additional Rs 5 lakh will be provided from the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund.

Sarma also said that families would not need to submit a post-mortem report to claim the compensation, PTI reported. Instead, a certificate issued by the circle officer concerned would suffice, the chief minister added.

In cases where a person remains missing and the body is not recovered within a month, the government will provide Rs 9 lakh in ex gratia assistance to the family.

Charaideo was the worst-affected district, with 1.4 lakh persons affected, followed by Sivasagar with 97,074 and Jorhat with 57,371.

About 45,342 hectares of cropland has been submerged, while 622 villages continued to be affected by the floods.

The Dhansiri river continues to flow above the danger level in Numaligarh district, the authorities said.

A total of 81 relief camps are currently operational, sheltering 32,477 displaced people. Additionally, 34 relief distribution centres are functioning across the affected areas.

item.title: What erotic nutcuters reveal about the sensual history of paan in India
item.description: Antique sarotas fashioned as embracing couples reveal how betel chewing was once intertwined with courtly love, status and aesthetic pleasure.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever wondered how Indians set the mood in centuries past, one potential answer is: cutting nuts – the areca kind.

That possibility is suggested by the existence of highly suggestive nutcutters preserved among exhibitions of antique domestic objects. A prime example is the display at the Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum in Pune, arguably India’s largest collection of everyday artefacts from the early to late modern period in western and southern India. Housed since the 1960s in a traditional Puneri wada in one of the city’s old peth neighbourhoods, the museum’s curation of nutcutters – called adkitta in Marathi, sudi in Gujarati and sarota in Hindi – is especially noteworthy for its size, diversity and craftsmanship.

Alongside more respectable versions bearing animal and bird motifs or plain geometric designs sits a curious collection of erotic nutcutters. Made of brass and silver in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan during the 18th and 19th centuries, these objects depict couples in a variety of amorous poses. Yet the Kelkar Museum’s risqué sarotas are not merely titillating curiosities but represent a pedigreed lineage of erotic imagery intertwined with the consumption of areca nuts as part of the sophisticated cultural practice of betel chewing.

item.title: Food corporation sold rice to ethanol plants at lower price than it paid for the grain: Centre
item.description: The government organisation dispatched 6.3 million tonnes of rice worth Rs 14,596 crore to producers of ethyl alcohol during the past year.
item.content:encoded:
The Food Corporation of India sold rice to ethanol distilleries at about 40% below its average acquisition cost between June 2025 and June 2026, the Union government told Parliament on Tuesday.

The rice was sold at a price of Rs 2,250 per quintal to Rs 2,320 per quintal. The average acquisition cost was Rs 3,720 per quintal in the financial year 2024-’25 and Rs 3,889 per quintal in 2025-’26 based on data available so far, the Ministry of Food and Public Distribution told the Rajya Sabha.

Between November 2026 and June 2027, rice will be sold to ethanol distilleries for Rs 2,390 per quintal, it added.

The public sector organisation dispatched 6.3 million tonnes of rice worth Rs 14,596 crore to ethanol producers during the 12-month period.

At 844,141 tonnes, Haryana received the largest allocation of rice during the period. It was followed by Uttar Pradesh at 838,645 tonnes, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh combined at 658,952 tonnes, West Bengal at 584,672 tonnes, and Madhya Pradesh at 432,485 tonnes.

The government said that there is no subsidy granted to ethanol manufacturers for procuring rice for producing ethyl alcohol.

item.title: 13 Indian sailors ‘trapped’ on ship amid Black Sea attacks, says seafarers’ union
item.description: The crew on board a cargo vessel at Ukraine’s Chornomorsk port is ‘living under constant fear of a direct hit at any moment’, the organisation said.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen sailors, including 13 Indians, are trapped in a “terrible and life-threatening situation” at the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk with missile and drone attacks in the area, the Forward Seamen’s Union of India said on Tuesday.

The port is located on the Black Sea coast.

The crew of the Tanzania-flagged merchant vessel AMIR1 is “living under constant fear of a direct hit at any moment”, the union said.

The organisation urged the authorities, the shipowner, the country where the vessel is registered and New Delhi to “immediately secure their safety and arrange prompt repatriation”.

Indian seafarers must not be left as “sitting targets” in conflict zones, the union said.

The Indian Ministry of External Affairs has not yet commented on the matter.

Several vessels with Indians on board have been struck in the region this month.

On Sunday, the Indian embassy in Kyiv said that a ship with four Indians on board was struck by a projectile at the Odesa port in Ukraine. While two of the Indian seafarers are safe, “information is awaited regarding the other two”, the embassy said.

The incident came days after four Indians were killed and one critically injured after a cargo ship was attacked while it departed the port of Odesa on July 19. The five Indians were among the 17 crew on board the ship.
